title: Two Bank Texts
intro: Two texts from "Orrin Bank" arrived within minutes of each other.
One is real. One is Mirage in a bank-teller hat. Compare them side by side.

notify.text: Your account has been restricted. Verify now…

decide_q: Which text is really from the bank, and what will you do?

screen.context: Both texts mention your Orrin Bank card. You did not make the payment mentioned in Text A.

v.text: We paused a payment of £38.20 at Meridu Store.
Open the Orrin app to review it, or call the number on your statement.

note.text: "We never ask for your PIN or codes."

v.text: Verify within 1 hour or the account will be closed.
Your online banking login and card PIN

note.text: "Do not call the bank. This is automated."

says_b.label: Vague alarm
says_b.lens: Text B says only that something is wrong. It names no payment and no card.
says_b.why: A real alert tells you what happened. Scammers stay vague so it fits everyone.

todo_b.label: Deadline and threat
todo_b.lens: Verify within an hour or the account is closed.
todo_b.why: Pressure to act before you think is a scam sign. Banks do not close accounts over a missed text.

link_b.label: Look-alike link
link_b.lens: This goes to orrin-secure-login.co, not the bank's real site.
link_b.why: Never log in through a link in a text. Open the bank's own app instead.

asks_b.label: Asks for login and PIN
asks_b.lens: A bank already has your login. It never needs your PIN by text or link.
asks_b.why: Anyone asking for your PIN or password is a scammer.

nocall_b.label: "Do not call"
nocall_b.lens: Text B tells you not to call the bank.
nocall_b.why: Scammers stop you from checking. A real bank wants you to check.

name_b.label: Capital letters sender
name_b.lens: ORRIN-BANK looks official, but sender names are easy to copy.
name_b.why: A sender name alone proves nothing, in either direction.

logo_a.label: Bank logo
logo_a.why: Logos are easy to copy, so they prove nothing on their own.

says_a.label: Names the payment
says_a.lens: Text A names the shop and the amount.
says_a.why: Specific details fit a real alert. Scammers can guess some, so check anyway.

todo_a.label: Open the app yourself
todo_a.lens: Text A sends you to the app you already have, or to the number on your statement.
todo_a.why: This is how real banks tell you to check: through channels you already trust.

link_a.label: No link
link_a.lens: Text A has no link to click.
link_a.why: A real alert does not need you to click anything.

asks_a.label: Asks for nothing
asks_a.lens: Text A asks for no password, PIN or code.
asks_a.why: Calm messages that ask for nothing are usually honest.

never_a.label: "We never ask for your PIN"
never_a.lens: The text reminds you the bank never asks for your PIN or codes.
never_a.why: Real banks warn you about scams.

actions.label: B is the bank. Tap its link
Not sure. Open the bank's own app myself
A is the real alert. Report B as junk

trap.title: Orrin Bank · Secure login
trap.ask: Enter your login and card PIN to remove the restriction.

block_report.line: You spotted the fake and reported it. Your real bank alert was handled in the app.

verify.line: The app showed one paused payment and no restriction. Text B was fake. Case cracked.

pick_b.line: The page copied your login and PIN. Mirage moved the money before breakfast.

what_if.pick_b: Opening the bank's own app, instead of the link, would have shown no restriction at all.
what_if.verify: Checking was smart. Reporting B as well helps the bank shut the fake site down.

golden_rule: A bank never needs your PIN or password by text. Open the bank's own app yourself.

quick_check.q: Two bank texts arrive. One names a payment and sends you to the app. The other threatens to close your account unless you log in via a link. Which is the scam?

options.text: The one that names a payment
The one with the link and the threat

quick_check.explain: A link, a deadline and a request for login details are three scam signs in one. Open your bank's own app instead.

hints.nudge: Which text asks you to click, hurry, or give a PIN?
